extracted.intended_audience: readers of philosophy and aesthetics; students and scholars interested in theories of comedy, tragedy, and art
extracted.subtask_description: Philosophical-aesthetic observations about the source and structure of amusement and pity/joy in art: how concealment, revelation, and preceding suffering shape comic and tragic effects. Relevant to writers, dramatists, and theorists of humor and narrative emotion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Source of the amusing
rubrics_metrics.description: "The source of the amusing is simply the constant concealment of the chief concern."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Amusement arises when a central concern or 'secret' is continually concealed while remaining present to thought; the audience understands the omitted matter by allusion, and this tension between knowledge and concealment produces the comic effect. Example/illustration in the text: sexual matters are an 'open secret'—never distinctly mentioned yet always understood. Anti-pattern: explicitly stating the chief concern removes the tension and diminishes amusement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allusion rather than explicit statement (the open secret)
rubrics_metrics.description: "It is the great αρρητον, the open secret, which must never and nowhere be distinctly mentioned, but always and everywhere is understood... the slightest allusion to it is instantly understood."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When treating taboo or powerful subjects (the text uses sexual generation as the example), imply rather than spell out; leave the principal matter unsaid but clearly signalled by context so the audience supplies it. This preserves psychological immediacy and comedic or dramatic tension. Anti-patterns: overt, blunt description that removes implication and the audience's contributory role.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aesthetic necessity: misery precedes great joy
rubrics_metrics.description: "Great and lively joy can only be conceived as the consequence of great misery... all poets are obliged to bring their heroes into anxious and painful situations, so that they may be able to free them from them. Dramas and Epics accordingly always describe only fighting, suffering, tormented men; and every romance is a rareeshow in which we observe the spasms and convulsions of the agonised human heart."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To produce strong positive emotional responses (catharsis, jubilant resolution, or powerful laughter), narrative art typically places characters in significant suffering or danger first; the contrast makes subsequent relief or joy intense and perceivable. Practical implication for writers: construct stakes, suffering, or conflict that the audience will feel, then resolve or invert them to yield intensified emotional payoff. Anti-pattern: maintaining constant, unvarying well-being (permanent satisfaction) produces little dramatic or comic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pleasure is experienced as negative; pain as positive
rubrics_metrics.description: "We feel pain, but not painlessness; we feel care, but not the absence of care... Well-being, on the other hand, is merely negative."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Psychological asymmetry: pain and want register positively in consciousness, whereas pleasures are experienced as mere negations and are noticed mainly in their absence. For creators, this means art's power often derives from depicting suffering or lack (which registers strongly), and using removal or inversion of that suffering to signal pleasure. Use contrasts (boredom vs. suffering, anticipation vs. fulfilment) to make pleasures perceptible. Anti-pattern: assuming pleasure alone will produce noticeable, sustained emotional engagement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of revelation on the innocent intellect
rubrics_metrics.description: Passage describing how the 'young, innocent, human intellect' is "startled at the enormity" when a great secret of the world becomes known to it, producing horror or astonishment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The psychological reaction of naive or unprepared consciousness to the disclosure of concealed truths can be used as a device: in comedy the startled recognition can yield amusement; in tragic or philosophical modes it produces horror or existential dread. Manage the audience's knowledge state (what is known vs. what is concealed) to control whether revelation reads as comic (incongruous/startling) or tragic (horrifying/profound). Anti-pattern: failing to calibrate audience information so revelations land with the intended emotional valence.
